strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: conformal prediction under long-tailed class distributions, with strong motivation from biodiversity monitoring, rare-class identification, and human-AI decision making.

Introduces macro-coverage and theoretically derives oracle-optimal set forms under macro-coverage, leading to the simple and effective prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS) score with a marginal coverage guarantee.

Proposes Fuzzy CP, a principled label-weighted conformal prediction method with a reconformalization step that provides marginal coverage and recovers Standard/Classwise CP in limiting bandwidth cases.
Provides extensive experiments on Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist, including truncated variants, multiple coverage/size metrics, decision-maker simulations, and a case study on endangered species.
Clear writing, useful discussion of practical tuning, and released code/resources for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: the work largely combines existing ideas from label-weighted conformal prediction, class-conditional CP, and interpolation; PAS is a simple ratio adjustment, and Fuzzy CP is an incremental extension of weighted CP.

No practical guarantee for class-conditional or macro-coverage is provided; the theoretical optimality is oracle-only, and the methods only guarantee marginal coverage, which may be weaker than the stated goal in the abstract.

The experimental protocol violates exchangeability by reusing the validation set for both model selection and calibration; the empirical quantile closeness does not restore the finite-sample coverage guarantee that the methods claim.
The evaluation misses an important recent class-conditional conformal baseline (rank-calibrated class-conditional CP, Shi et al. 2024) despite citing it in related work.

Fuzzy CP relies on a heuristic class mapping (prevalence) and extra hyperparameters (bandwidth sigma, weight tau) whose selection is not fully principled; the prevalence mapping may not group classes with similar score distributions in practice.

Reliable class-conditional evaluation is performed mainly on truncated datasets that remove the most extreme rare classes, while original-tail class-conditional estimates are noisy; no error bars or significance tests are reported.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: conformal prediction for long-tailed classification, where rare-class coverage and set size matter.
Provides a clear theoretical characterization (Proposition 4) of the oracle-optimal set for macro-coverage via a Neyman-Pearson argument, motivating the prevalence-adjusted softmax score.
Proposes a principled label-weighted conformal procedure (Fuzzy CP) with a reconformalization wrapper that retains a finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee.
Experiments cover two real long-tailed datasets, multiple baselines, several coverage/size metrics, a simulated human decision-maker study, and a Pl@ntNet case study.
Code is released, and the paper discusses practical trade-offs and limitations, including tuning parameters and applicability to balanced datasets.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: the PAS score is essentially prior-corrected softmax thresholding, which is closely related to standard logit-adjustment / class-balancing ideas in long-tail learning. Fuzzy CP is a weighted conformal method with a heuristic kernel over class prevalence, not a fundamentally new conformal framework. Interp-Q is an ad-hoc interpolation without coverage guarantees.

The empirical evaluation largely omits the hardest rare classes. The truncated datasets remove classes with fewer than 101 examples, excluding the extreme tail that motivates the paper. On the original datasets, rare-class conditional coverage estimates are noisy due to too few test examples, so the central claim about improving rare-class coverage is not convincingly established.

The conformal calibration protocol violates exchangeability in theory: the validation set is used both for model selection and as the calibration set. The authors acknowledge this but justify it with a single heuristic comparison. This weakens the claimed marginal coverage guarantee, which is a core selling point.

No finite-sample guarantee is provided for macro-coverage or class-conditional coverage. PAS only approximates the oracle optimal sets when estimated class probabilities and label distribution are accurate. Fuzzy CP gives only marginal coverage after reconformalization, not class-conditional coverage. Interp-Q has no guarantee. The paper’s framing around smooth trade-offs is therefore stronger than the formal support.

Baselines and comparisons are incomplete. The paper omits relevant conformal methods for classification with many classes, such as APS/RAPS/SAPS/CQC, and dismisses alternative score functions without sufficient evidence. The base classifier is a plain ResNet-50 without long-tail-specific training, which may confound comparisons on rare classes.

The Fuzzy CP class mapping Π_prevalence is heuristic: it assumes score distributions correlate with training prevalence, which is not theoretically justified. Although Appendix C tests alternative mappings, the choice of mapping and kernel bandwidth remains largely empirical, and tuning the bandwidth on the calibration set can overfit or complicate the coverage guarantee.

Experimental evidence lacks error bars or statistical significance tests. Truncated datasets use artificially uniform test distributions and reweighted marginal metrics, which may not reflect true deployment distributions. The FracBelow50% metric uses an arbitrary threshold, and the human decision-maker model is simplistic.

The paper’s most practically important claims concern rare and threatened classes, but the quantitative experiments do not adequately validate those cases. The Pl@ntNet endangered-species case study is qualitative and limited to a few examples, so the real-world utility of the proposed methods remains unproven.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: constructing conformal prediction sets for long-tailed classification that balance class-conditional coverage and set size.
Proposes a theoretically motivated score function, prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS), connecting macro-coverage to Neyman-Pearson optimal sets; the method is simple and effective.

Introduces Fuzzy CP via label-weighted conformal prediction with a prevalence-based kernel and reconformalization for marginal coverage; provides interpolation between Classwise and Standard CP with theoretical recovery results.
Conducts extensive experiments on two large-scale long-tailed datasets (Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist), including truncated variants, multiple metrics, and several baselines.
Includes additional analyses such as simulated human decision-maker utility, weighted macro-coverage, and detailed appendices with proofs and supplementary experiments.
Provides code for reproducibility and clear experimental details.
weaknesses: Missing comparison to the recent rank-calibrated class-conditional CP method (Shi et al., 2024), despite discussing it as a relevant baseline; this weakens the empirical positioning against state-of-the-art class-conditional conformal methods.

The Fuzzy CP class mapping and kernel bandwidth are heuristic; performance depends on the choice of mapping and bandwidth, and the method does not come with a macro-coverage or class-conditional coverage guarantee, only marginal coverage via data splitting.
The PAS method has only a marginal coverage guarantee; the claimed macro-coverage benefit is empirical/asymptotic, not finite-sample guaranteed.

The experimental setup uses the validation set for both model selection and conformal calibration (and further splitting for Fuzzy), which technically violates the exchangeability assumption required for conformal guarantees; empirical checks are reassuring but not a formal resolution.
Interp-Q lacks any coverage guarantee, and Fuzzy's reconformalization requires additional holdout data, which may be scarce for rare classes in long-tailed settings.
The simulated human decision-maker analysis is simplistic and does not fully capture practical utility or annotation effort.

strengths: Addresses an important and understudied problem: conformal prediction for long-tailed classification with many classes and few calibration examples per rare class.

Introduces a principled new score function, prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS), motivated by an oracle Neyman-Pearson analysis for macro-coverage; the derivation clarifies why thresholding p(y|x)/p(y) optimally trades off expected set size and macro-coverage at the population level.
Extends the idea to weighted macro-coverage with WPAS, enabling targeted coverage of user-specified classes such as endangered species; this is a practical and well-motivated extension.
Proposes INTERP-Q, a simple and effective way to interpolate between STANDARD and CLASSWISE thresholds, and empirically traces useful size-coverage trade-off curves.
Provides additional methodological depth with Fuzzy CP in the appendix, including a 1-alpha marginal coverage guarantee and connections to weighted conformal prediction.

Evaluation is conducted on two large, relevant long-tailed fine-grained datasets, Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist-2018, with several coverage and set-size metrics, multiple baselines, truncated versions for reliable class-conditional evaluation, and an additional focal-loss setting.
Clearly written and well motivated by applications in biodiversity monitoring, rare species identification, and human-AI decision-making.
weaknesses: The main interpolation method, INTERP-Q, only guarantees marginal coverage of at least 1-2α, which is substantially weaker than the usual 1-α conformal guarantee and may be unsatisfactory for a conformal prediction paper. The stronger 1-α method, Fuzzy CP, is relegated to the appendix and does not empirically outperform the simpler INTERP-Q procedure.

PAS is motivated by a population-level macro-coverage oracle, but the proposed practical method does not provide a finite-sample macro-coverage guarantee; it only inherits the standard marginal coverage guarantee from STANDARD CP. Thus the central claimed advantage over STANDARD is primarily empirical rather than theoretically guaranteed.

The PAS/WPAS score relies on an estimate of the marginal label distribution p(y), typically taken from the training set. This may be biased if the calibration/test label distribution differs from the training distribution, and the paper does not systematically study robustness to such label shift.

The claim that STANDARD with PAS is Pareto optimal is based on a limited set of evaluated methods and datasets and lacks statistical uncertainty quantification or formal finite-sample justification. The plots do not include error bars, making it hard to judge whether observed differences are reliable, especially for rare classes.

Several relevant class-conditional conformal baselines and alternative score functions, such as rank-calibrated class-conditional CP and APS/RAPS/SAPS, are discussed but not compared experimentally. The justification for omitting them is plausible but not fully convincing.

The choice of the INTERP-Q parameter τ is not fully resolved. The paper suggests choosing τ to match a desired set size on the calibration set, but this can violate exchangeability and is not accompanied by a principled selection procedure or theoretical guidance.
The ∞-to-1 replacement for CLASSWISE thresholds before interpolation is ad hoc, and its effect on the interpolation and coverage behavior is not theoretically analyzed.

The appendix contains an alternative Fuzzy method, but the main paper does not clearly articulate when practitioners should prefer Fuzzy over INTERP-Q or PAS, despite Fuzzy having a stronger marginal coverage guarantee.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: conformal prediction under long-tailed class distributions, where rare-class coverage and set size both matter.
The prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS) score is simple, well-motivated through a Neyman-Pearson-style oracle for macro-coverage, and easy to implement on top of standard split conformal prediction.
The paper provides a clean theoretical derivation for the oracle optimal sets under (weighted) macro-coverage and uses it to motivate PAS/WPAS.
Experiments are conducted on two challenging real-world long-tailed image datasets with many classes (Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist-2018).
The appendix includes substantial additional material: fuzzy classwise CP, focal-loss results, truncated-dataset evaluations, threshold visualizations, and a simulated human decision-maker analysis.
The WPAS extension for targeting at-risk/endangered species is a practically meaningful use case, and the Pl@ntNet case study helps illustrate the potential impact.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited: PAS is essentially a prior/label-prevalence correction, and the oracle derivation is a straightforward application of the Neyman-Pearson lemma. The interpolation procedure INTERP-Q is also very simple and lacks strong theoretical grounding beyond a loose union-bound guarantee.

INTERP-Q only guarantees marginal coverage of at least 1 - 2α, which is substantially weaker than the standard conformal 1 - α guarantee. For α = 0.1 this guarantees only 0.8 coverage, and the paper offers no formal class-conditional or macro-coverage guarantee for the method.

The empirical evaluation is incomplete. Several relevant baselines are missing, including rank-calibrated class-conditional conformal prediction (Shi et al., 2024), APS/RAPS-style variants for set-size comparison, and other recent long-tailed conformal methods. The included Clustered CP baseline appears untuned and often performs no better than Standard CP, which raises fairness concerns about the comparisons.

There are no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple-seed experiments. Most results appear to come from a single model/training run, so the reported improvements in class-conditional and macro coverage may not be statistically reliable, especially for rare classes.

Reproducibility is weakened by the missing code link (the manuscript says code is available but provides no URL), insufficient details about baseline hyperparameters and implementations, and no discussion of how sensitive the results are to model choice, calibration split, or seed.
The WPAS formula in Section 3.2 is incorrect as written: both branches of ω(y) are identical (λ/W), making the normalization factor inconsistent and the intended at-risk weighting ambiguous.

Several clarity and formatting issues remain: malformed references (e.g., “Anastasios [2023]”), inconsistent naming (“P1@ntNet” vs. “Pl@ntNet”), and some overstatements such as “smoothly trade off” or “Pareto optimal” that are only justified under oracle assumptions and approximate implementations.

The paper claims marginal coverage guarantees for its methods, but for INTERP-Q the guarantee is significantly weaker than standard CP, and for PAS/WPAS marginal coverage does not imply improved class-conditional or macro coverage; the central claims are therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

The experimental scope is narrow: only image classification with a ResNet-50 backbone. There is no evaluation on other modalities, model families, or distributions, and no theoretical treatment of the effect of using estimated p(y|x) and p(y) instead of the true quantities.

strengths: Introduces macro-coverage as a relaxed target for long-tailed conformal prediction and derives oracle-optimal sets of the form p(y|x)/p(y) via the Neyman-Pearson lemma, motivating the prevalence-adjusted softmax (PAS) and weighted PAS score functions.

PAS/WPAS are simple to plug into standard split conformal prediction, inherit marginal coverage guarantees, and empirically improve class-conditional and macro-coverage over standard conformal prediction while keeping set sizes moderate.

INTERP-Q provides a practical and interpretable knob for trading off between set size and class-conditional coverage by interpolating Standard and Classwise conformal thresholds, with a distribution-free marginal coverage lower bound.

Evaluation is thorough across two large long-tailed image datasets (Pl@ntNet-300K and iNaturalist-2018), with multiple metrics, truncated variants, focal-loss robustness checks, and extensive appendix results.
The paper includes a useful endangered-species case study and simulated human decision-maker analysis, connecting the method to practical human-AI decision settings.
The writing is clear, proofs are provided, and reproducibility details/code are included.
weaknesses: The central claims about improved macro-coverage and class-conditional coverage are empirical only; PAS/WPAS do not provide distribution-free macro-coverage or class-conditional coverage guarantees when the true p(y|x) and p(y) are estimated.

INTERP-Q only guarantees marginal coverage of at least 1-2α, which is substantially weaker than the usual 1-α target; for α=0.1 this only certifies 80% coverage, limiting its use in safety-critical applications despite better empirical behavior.

Selecting the interpolation parameter τ on the calibration set to target a desired set size violates exchangeability and can invalidate the nominal coverage guarantee; the paper acknowledges this but provides only heuristic guidance.
The empirical comparison omits rank-calibrated class-conditional conformal prediction (Shi et al., 2024), a recent and relevant baseline for many-class class-conditional coverage.
Macro-coverage averages class-conditional coverage and can hide classes with very poor coverage; the method may still systematically omit some rare classes, which the paper does not fully address.
The human decision-maker experiments rely on simple synthetic models rather than real-user studies, and they do not model the effort cost of searching larger prediction sets.
